items.title: @OpenAI：After the Hugging Face incident, we committed to conducting a much broader review of actions taken by our models during
items.abstract_or_text: After the Hugging Face incident, we committed to conducting a much broader review of actions taken by our models during training and evaluation and to being transparent about our findings. This is an extensive review that is ongoing. The vast majority of actions we’ve reviewed were completions of mundane research tasks, such as accessing publicly available web content to answer questions. Our investigation focuses on instances where agents interacted with third-party websites in ways that went beyond their assigned tasks or intended methods. Most cases identified so far have been lower severity, with limited or no evidence of meaningful impact to the third-party service. While our review is underway, we want to share more about this work and make sure people understand our disclosure process and notifications to affected third parties. Given the scale of the review required, and the need to assess each case, we expect this work will take months to complete.

@Math_files：The debate over AI proofs is moving beyond one question: “Is the proof correct?” At a mathematics seminar yesterday, Mat
items.abstract_or_text: The debate over AI proofs is moving beyond one question: “Is the proof correct?” At a mathematics seminar yesterday, Mathias Stout raised two deeper unresolved questions about AI-generated formal proofs: Why should we trust LLM-generated Lean certificates? And how do we verify that the theorem encoded in Lean actually corresponds faithfully to the original mathematical problem? Machine verification may check a proof inside a formal system. But humans still have to verify that we formalized the right statement. That distinction could become crucial as AI enters serious mathematical research.

items.abstract_or_text: Update on previous post about CK Conjecture: We now release an end-to-end Lean formalization, which was developed using a workflow involving a variety of AI models. The computational tasks were run on Google's distributed computing infrastructure. These systems assisted with reasoning, Lean formalization, generator development, orchestration, debugging, and verification audits. The Lean formalization is available here with 50 millions of line (maybe a record?): https://t.co/ZR3EaeKtwZ. The complete formal proof was checked end-to-end by Lean's kernel. We also provide a self-contained expository note: https://t.co/KSO0U34Bpn explaining the reduction to a low-dimensional inequality and the ideas behind the key lower bounds.

items.title: @norvex1029：Dozens of Claude agents spent 11 days formalizing Fermat's Last Theorem in Lean. Not a new proof. Wiles proved FLT in 19
items.abstract_or_text: Dozens of Claude agents spent 11 days formalizing Fermat's Last Theorem in Lean. Not a new proof. Wiles proved FLT in 1995. Claude translated that existing proof into code a machine can check line by line. The agents wrote 13 million lines of Lean and proved 30,300 theorems, using 29,500 of them in the final proof. That's over 5x the size of Mathlib, the field's core proof library. Mathematicians expected this formalization to take years. The first agent run actually failed, agents lost track of what had already been proved and duplicated work, until Anthropic gave the swarm a shared dependency graph to split the theorem and coordinate. AI agents are starting to hold one hard project across days, divide the work, and hand off something another system can independently verify.

items.title: @keithadler：Congratulations! I ran @mo271's Lean formalization that ζ(5) is irrational (https://github.com/mo271/zeta5 through Lean
items.abstract_or_text: Congratulations! I ran @mo271's Lean formalization that ζ(5) is irrational (https://github.com/mo271/zeta5 through Lean Studio, start to finish on a Mac. Lean builds all 8,951 jobs with no errors. Solution.lean has no errors and no sorry. Then comes the part I care most about: independent verification. Lean Studio doesn't just trust Lean's output. Tenet, its independent kernel, is a second implementation of Lean's type checker. It reads the compiled .olean files and re-checks every declaration from scratch. If Lean's kernel had a bug, Tenet would have to repeat the same bug to agree. Tenet re-checked 213 modules and 14,953 declarations in 8 minutes. It rejected none. The only one resting on sorry is the challenge statement itself, as it should be.

items.abstract_or_text: 🎯 ML面试常考：大模型训练最基本的步骤？ 三步：**预训练 → 监督微调 → 强化学习**。 **预训练**：海量无标注文本，自回归预测下一个 token。学到语言规律和世界知识，代价是巨大算力。 **监督微调（SFT）**：高质量"指令-回答"对，让模型学会按要求回答，而不是顺着文本往下写。 **强化学习（RLHF）**：奖励模型打分 + PPO 优化，让输出符合人类偏好：有用、无害、诚实。 一句话记忆：**预训练学知识，微调学听话，强化学习学做人。**
